summary:
Project Summary
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) data into real time sound. Built by Walnut Space for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it pairs visual climate indicators global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest loss, and ice sheet mass change with dynamic sonification generated in the browser using the Web Audio API.
Users select a dataset, choose a musical scale and synth timbre, adjust tempo, and scrub a timeline from the 1990s to the present. Data values are mapped to pitch and pacing so rising seas climb in frequency, growing CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass decline falls in descending arpeggios. A live Canvas waveform runs alongside the audio.
The project addresses the challenge by making complex Earth science multi-sensory and accessible especially for blind and low vision users while keeping the underlying science intact. Hearing planetary change, not only seeing it, strengthens engagement, memory, and emotional connection, supporting education, outreach, and inclusive climate communication.
details:
Project Details

 

 What it does and how it works   

Earth Jukebox is a browser-based application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) climate indicators into real-time sound. Users choose one of four datasets—global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest cover loss, or ice-sheet mass change—then select a musical scale (pentatonic minor, major, harmonic minor, or chromatic), synthesizer timbre (sine, triangle, sawtooth, square), and tempo. A timeline scrubber moves from the 1990s to the present. As data values change, the Web Audio API maps them to pitch and pacing: rising sea level climbs in frequency, higher CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass loss falls in descending arpeggios. A Canvas waveform updates live beside the audio so sighted users see and hear the same trend.

 

 Benefits and intended impact   

The project makes Earth science multi-sensory and more accessible, especially for blind and low-vision users who are often excluded by visualization-only tools. Hearing planetary change can strengthen emotional connection and memory compared with numbers or charts alone. It is suited to classrooms, museums, and public outreach, where an interactive “jukebox” of Earth’s data can support teaching and engagement without requiring specialized hardware.

 

 Tools and technologies   

Built entirely as a client-side web app using HTML5, Vanilla JavaScript, the Web Audio API (oscillators, gain envelopes, scheduling), HTML5 Canvas for the waveform, and Tailwind CSS for a dark cosmic interface. No server or extra hardware is required beyond a modern browser and speakers or headphones.

 

 Creativity and design considerations   

Creativity lies in assigning each dataset a distinct sonic character that reflects its physical meaning, and in giving users control over scale, timbre, and tempo so the same data can be explored as different musical moods. The team prioritized accessibility (clear labels, descriptive text, keyboard-friendly controls), scientific integrity (parameter mapping tied to real indicator trends), and simplicity (lightweight stack, no plugins) so the experience works widely and stays focused on hearing Earth’s change.
